analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and senior officials from trading stocks and serving on corporate boards.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to five House committees, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar senior government officials — including members of Congress, their spouses, and executive branch officials at GS-14 level or higher — from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, or futures, from taking short positions against securities, and from serving as officers or board members of for-profit companies. Officials could keep holdings they had before taking office if they placed them in a qualified blind trust or sold them within six months. Knowing violations would carry a civil penalty of at least 10% of the value of the trade.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer face the risk that lawmakers making policy on an industry are simultaneously betting on or invested in that industry's stocks. It also protects constituents from officials sitting on corporate boards while regulating those companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits covered officials from buying or selling securities, commodities, or futures, including through synthetic derivatives, and from creating net short positions in securities.

It bars covered officials from serving as an officer or board member of any for-profit corporation or association, closing a channel where officials could hold paid corporate positions while shaping policy affecting those companies.

The ban covers not just members of Congress but also their spouses and a broad range of executive branch officials — political appointees, Senior Executive Service employees, and anyone at GS-14 or above — closing common routes around a members-only rule.
Knowing violations carry a civil penalty of at least 10% of the value of the trade, giving the ban financial teeth rather than relying on disclosure alone.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, along with thousands of senior executive branch officials, who would have to divest individual holdings, place them in blind trusts, and give up corporate board seats and short-position strategies.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement would run through the House and Senate Ethics Committees — the bodies made up of, and policing, the very members subject to the ban — and the only penalty specified is a civil fine of at least 10% of the transaction value, with no criminal exposure written into the bill.

The ban reaches every federal employee at GS-14 or above and the entire Senior Executive Service, a population of thousands of career civil servants, which could complicate recruiting and retaining experienced financial and legal professionals in government.

The exceptions allow officials to keep pre-existing holdings in blind trusts, so members could remain invested in the overall market; the bill targets active trading and short positions rather than ownership itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the conflict of interest when officials trade the stocks of companies they regulate or legislate on — is real and goes to the public. The costs fall almost entirely on the officials themselves, which is the point. The bill's weakest spot is enforcement: it leaves policing to the ethics committees of the very chambers whose members would be restricted, and the civil-penalty approach gives violators little to fear beyond a fine. The breadth of the ban (all GS-14+ employees, not just lawmakers) is a defensible design choice but one an honest supporter would acknowledge as an administrative burden on career staff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever held a hearing or marked it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard introduced the Integrity for Public Officials Act on April 7, 2020.
The bill was referred to five committees — Financial Services, Agriculture, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary — but no committee took any further action on it.
The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party.
The bill would have prohibited senior officials including members of Congress from trading securities, commodities, and futures, taking short positions, and serving on for-profit boards.

It allowed exceptions for holdings placed in qualified blind trusts or divested within six months of taking office, and set a civil penalty of at least 10% of the transaction value for knowing violations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress, their spouses, and senior executive branch officials are better off: they kept the ability to trade individual stocks and commodities and to sit on corporate boards, and the pre-existing disclosure-only framework remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and senior officials

for.name: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the IPO Act, banning senior officials from securities trading and for-profit board service.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Agriculture, House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Received split referrals and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern took shape.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would have stripped them of the ability to trade individual stocks, commodities, and futures and to hold for-profit board seats. Their interest in keeping those financial activities runs against the public's interest in officials without personal stakes in the policies they write.

industries.industry: Senior executive branch officials (GS-14 and above, SES, and political appointees)
industries.note: Thousands of career and appointed officials would have had to divest or blind-trust their holdings. Their interest in maintaining active trading rights runs against transparency in government decision-making.
